summary: DNSSEC resolvers need trust anchors to validate responses, and many will need to update them automatically. This document lists the requirements that an automated trust anchor rollover method must meet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The first key you trust has to be swapped sometimes. This lists what a safe swap must do.

subtitle: The checklist any automated method for updating DNSSEC trust anchors must satisfy.

tldr.problem: Every DNSSEC-aware resolver needs trust anchors to validate answers, and manually updating them will not scale across the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists requirements for an automated, specification-based trust anchor rollover method, such as scalability, support for planned and emergency rollovers, and recovery from compromise.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol itself. It gives a consistent yardstick to measure proposed rollover mechanisms.

today: RFC 4986 is an Informational requirements document that has not been obsoleted or updated according to its metadata. It sets criteria and does not itself define a rollover protocol.

sections.title: Why Trust Anchors Need Rollover
sections.content:
DNSSEC lets a security-aware resolver check DNS records, starting from one or more trust anchors that it holds. Getting those anchors in the first place, in a trustworthy way, is out of scope here, and entering them is often a manual step.

For some environments, manual management is fine. Many others need an automated, specification-based method to update trust anchors. This document supplies a list of requirements to measure any proposed automated method consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: A trust anchor is like the one person you believe without asking anyone else. Sometimes that person's badge expires, so you need a safe way to learn about the new badge.

sections.title: Background and Definitions
sections.content:
A resolver needs starting points. Stub resolvers normally start from IP addresses of recursive name servers, and recursive servers from root server addresses. For DNSSEC, the starting point is one or more DNSKEY or DS records, each called a Trust Anchor.

A DNSKEY or DS record is not a trust anchor just because a zone operator publishes it. It becomes one when a resolver operator decides to use it, so the zone operator may not know who uses it. The obvious exception is the Root Zone keys. Responsibility for the validity of the chosen anchors lies with the resolver operator.

The document also defines related terms: Initial Trust Relationship, Trust Anchor Distribution, Trust Anchor Maintenance (adding, deleting or replacing an anchor), Revocation and Removal, Rollover, and the planned versus emergency forms of rollover and revocation. Manual rollover, as early adopters publish their processes, will not scale, which motivates the automated approach.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a list of people you have decided to trust. Only you can say who is on it, so you are also the one who must keep it up to date.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements use RFC 2119 words, and where trade-offs are needed, MUST requirements win over SHOULD, MAY or RECOMMENDED ones. Highlights:

  • Scalability (MUST): support Internet-wide use, including possibly very many resolvers embedded in applications, multiple zones, and multiple anchors per zone. The count per resolver is stated as less than 20 in most cases, but possibly as high as one thousand.
  • No known intellectual property encumbrance: the chosen solution must not be known to be encumbered, or must be available royalty-free.
  • General applicability and private networks (MUST): work for any zone, and support private networks with their own DNS hierarchy.
  • Stale anchor detection (MUST): a resolver must be able to detect that anchors can no longer be updated, and should tell the operator to reestablish initial trust.
  • Manual operations permitted: the protocol must allow both automated and manual maintenance.
  • Planned and unplanned rollovers (MUST).
  • Timeliness and high availability (SHOULD): distribute new and revoked records promptly and make their state available in a trustworthy way.
  • Maintenance operations (MUST): add, delete or replace an anchor.
  • Recovery from compromise (MUST): recover if at least one other uncompromised key is still configured for the zone.
  • Non-degrading trust (MUST): the rollover must not weaken the existing trust.

On new RR types or protocol changes, the document only says this should be considered when evaluating solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: A good way to swap trusted keys must work for lots of people, handle both planned and surprise swaps, notice when something went stale, and never make you trust less than before.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines overall requirements for an automated trust anchor rollover solution. It specifically does not define the security mechanisms needed to meet those requirements. Those are left to whichever solution is proposed and measured against this list.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper only writes the rules of the game. It does not say how to build the lock.
